title: Transactions and ACID in depth
scopeHtml: Scope: transactions, ACID mechanisms in Postgres, atomicity, constraints, durability and commit, long transactions, outbox and idempotency.

notes.title: What a transaction is
notes.html:
A transaction is a group of statements that the database treats as one unit: either all of them take effect, or none do. You open it with BEGIN, finish with COMMIT (keep everything) or ROLLBACK (throw everything away). Without BEGIN, Postgres wraps every single statement in its own tiny transaction (autocommit).

Why care? Moving money is two writes: subtract from A, add to B. If the server dies between them, money vanishes. A transaction makes the pair atomic.

Worked example. Transfer 100 from account 1 to account 2:

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

If the second UPDATE fails (constraint, crash, deadlock), the first is undone. In Postgres, an error inside a transaction puts it in an "aborted" state: every later statement fails with current transaction is aborted until you ROLLBACK (or use a SAVEPOINT, see below).

Industry examples. Stripe-style ledgers write debit and credit rows in one transaction. Instagram-style "create post" writes the post row, the feed fan-out job row and a counter in one transaction, then publishes the job from an outbox table.

Everyday analogy. Handing cash across a counter while the cashier hands you the item: both happen or the whole sale is cancelled. Nobody walks away with both.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "a transaction is a lock". It is a unit of work; locks are one mechanism inside it.
  • Forgetting autocommit: two separate statements in a script are NOT atomic unless you wrap them.
  • Not knowing that in Postgres even DDL (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE) is transactional and can be rolled back (MySQL cannot).

notes.title: ACID overview
notes.html:
ACID is four promises: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Each one is a separate mechanism.

Letter Promise Postgres mechanism
A All or nothing MVCC row versions plus the commit log (clog / pg_xact); aborted rows are simply invisible
C Data obeys the rules Constraints, triggers, foreign keys; the app defines the rules
I Concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work MVCC snapshots plus locks (files 07 and 08)
D Committed data survives a crash Write-ahead log flushed to disk (file 09)

Decision gravity. ACID is the default you pay for. You can relax individual letters: synchronous_commit = off relaxes D for speed (a crash can lose the last ~200 ms or so of commits, but never corrupts data); lower isolation relaxes I. These are reversible config changes. Choosing a database that does not give A across multiple keys (many NoSQL stores) is a heavier, one-way architectural choice.

Everyday analogy. Sending a registered parcel: it arrives whole (A), matches the order form (C), other parcels do not get mixed in (I), and there is a signed receipt even if the van later burns down (D).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating "Consistency" in ACID as the same as "consistency" in CAP. ACID-C means "rules hold"; CAP-C means "all replicas agree" (linearizability).
  • Saying the database guarantees consistency by itself. It enforces only the rules you declared.

notes.title: Atomicity in depth
notes.html:
Atomicity means a crash or error mid-transaction leaves no trace. Postgres does not undo changes; it never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE writes a NEW row version (tuple) and marks the old one as ended by this transaction ID (xmax). If the transaction aborts, readers consult the commit log, see "aborted", and ignore the new version. No undo log is replayed. (InnoDB differs: it changes in place and keeps an undo log.)

Each transaction gets a 32-bit transaction ID (xid) only when it first writes. Row headers store xmin (creator) and xmax (deleter). Visibility = "is xmin committed and visible to my snapshot, and is xmax not."

heap page, row for account 1
version 1: xmin=100 xmax=205  balance=500   <- ended by tx 205
version 2: xmin=205 xmax=0    balance=400   <- new
if tx 205 aborts: version 2 is ignored, version 1 is alive again

Savepoints give partial rollback inside a transaction:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders ...;
SAVEPOINT s1;
INSERT INTO order_items ...;   -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1;      -- order row kept, items undone
COMMIT;

ORMs use savepoints for "nested transactions". Each savepoint creates a subtransaction; more than 64 live subtransactions per backend overflow a cache and have caused real slowdowns on busy systems, so do not wrap every loop iteration in one.

Industry examples. Postgres's no-undo design makes rollback instant even for a huge transaction (abort is just a flag), but leaves dead rows behind for VACUUM. Oracle and InnoDB make rollback slow instead, because they must apply undo.

Everyday analogy. Writing a draft on a fresh sheet and only swapping it into the folder at the end. If you abandon it, the old sheet is still there untouched.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Postgres uses an undo log. It uses versioned rows.
  • Forgetting that an aborted transaction still consumed space until vacuum cleans it.
  • Catching a SQL error in app code and carrying on in the same transaction without a savepoint; Postgres refuses further statements.

notes.title: Consistency and constraints
notes.html:
Consistency means every committed state satisfies the rules you declared. The database can only enforce rules it knows about, so declare them.

Constraint kinds: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, EXCLUDE (e.g. no two overlapping bookings for a room). Constraints can be DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, checked at COMMIT instead of per statement, which is needed for circular references or swapping two unique values.

CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  balance numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE TABLE booking (
  room int, during tstzrange,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)
);

Worked example. Two sessions both withdraw 80 from a balance of 100. With CHECK (balance >= 0) and an atomic UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = 1, the second blocks until the first commits, re-evaluates, sees 20, and the CHECK fails. The invariant holds with no extra code. But read-then-write in app code (SELECT then UPDATE balance = 20) can break rules that live only in app code.

Decision gravity. Put invariants in the database whenever you can: they survive every future client, script and bug. App-only validation is reversible but leaks. Adding a constraint to a big existing table needs care: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT avoids a long exclusive lock.

Everyday analogy. A form with required fields enforced by the website itself, not just by a polite note asking staff to double check.

Common interview traps.

  • Enforcing uniqueness with SELECT-then-INSERT in code (race condition); use a UNIQUE index and handle the violation.
  • Thinking foreign keys are free: they take locks on the parent row and cost writes. Still usually worth it.

notes.title: Durability and commit
notes.html:
Durability means once COMMIT returns, the data survives a power cut. Postgres achieves it by writing the change to the write-ahead log (WAL) and calling fsync before acknowledging. The heap pages themselves are flushed later (checkpoints). Details in file 09.

Settings that matter:

  • synchronous_commit = on (default): wait for WAL flush to local disk.
  • synchronous_commit = off: return before the flush; risk of losing the last few transactions (bounded by wal_writer_delay, 200 ms by default x about 3), but no corruption.
  • fsync = off: dangerous, can corrupt the whole cluster. Never in production.
  • With sync replicas: synchronous_commit = remote_apply waits until a standby has applied it.

Worked example. A cloud SSD fsync takes ~0.5 to 2 ms, so one session doing small commits sequentially tops out at roughly 500 to 2,000 commits/s. Group commit lets many sessions share one fsync, so 64 concurrent sessions can reach tens of thousands of commits/s. Batching 100 inserts per transaction cuts fsyncs 100x.

Industry examples. Stripe-style payment paths keep synchronous_commit = on with a synchronous replica. Analytics ingestion pipelines often use off for a table-heavy bulk load. Hardware matters: consumer SSDs that lie about fsync (no power-loss capacitors) break durability silently.

Everyday analogy. The receipt printed before you leave the shop. If the till computer crashes later, the paper receipt proves the sale happened.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing synchronous_commit = off can corrupt data. It can lose recent commits, not corrupt.
  • Saying COMMIT writes the table pages to disk. It writes the WAL.

notes.title: Autocommit, batching and long transactions
notes.html:
A transaction should be as short as it can be while still correct. Open a transaction, do the work, commit. Do not hold one open across a user's think time, an HTTP call or a queue wait.

Why long transactions hurt in Postgres:

  • They hold their snapshot, so VACUUM cannot remove dead rows newer than it (xmin horizon), causing bloat.
  • They hold locks, blocking others.
  • idle in transaction sessions keep all of the above while doing nothing.
-- find the offenders
SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;

-- guardrails (per role or database)
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE app SET statement_timeout = '15s';

Worked example (incident pattern). A report job opens a transaction at 02:00 and sits idle in transaction for 6 hours because the app crashed mid-way holding a connection. Meanwhile 5M rows churn; VACUUM runs but cannot reclaim them; table grows from 20 GB to 35 GB and index scans slow down. Symptom: rising table size, n_dead_tup climbing, autovacuum "running" constantly. Metric: oldest xact_start age.

Batching rule of thumb. Bulk loads: 1,000 to 10,000 rows per transaction, or use COPY (often 10x or more faster than row INSERTs). Row-by-row autocommit of 1M rows means 1M fsyncs.

Everyday analogy. Keeping a library book checked out for a year "just in case". Others cannot use it and the shelf cannot be reorganised.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a remote API inside an open DB transaction.
  • Not setting idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  • Forgetting connection poolers in transaction mode break session-level features (see file 10).

notes.title: Distributed work: outbox and idempotency
notes.html:
A database transaction cannot span "write to Postgres" and "send to Kafka". If you do both, one can succeed while the other fails. The transactional outbox fixes it: in the SAME transaction write your business row and a row into an outbox table; a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, marking rows done. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, total) VALUES (42, 7, 99.00);
INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, type, payload)
VALUES (42, 'OrderCreated', '{"id":42,"total":99.00}');
COMMIT;
-- relay: SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id
--        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100;

Idempotency key. Client sends a unique key (e.g. Idempotency-Key: pay_abc123). A UNIQUE constraint on it means a retry hits a unique violation and you return the saved result instead of charging twice.

Industry examples. Stripe documents idempotency keys for payments. Debezium reads the Postgres WAL and publishes outbox rows to Kafka (change data capture) without polling.

Decision gravity. Outbox is a safe, boring default; dual writes are a one-way bug factory. Alternatives: 2PC (heavy, file 11) or sagas (compensating steps, more app logic).

Everyday analogy. Writing "send this letter" in your own diary at the same moment you pay for the stamp; a clerk later posts every diary entry. If the clerk repeats one, the receiver ignores duplicates.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual write: save, then publish, no outbox.
  • Saying exactly-once delivery exists end to end. You get at-least-once plus idempotent consumers.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit; autocommit makes every lone statement its own transaction.
  • ACID: A via versioned rows plus commit status, C via declared constraints, I via MVCC and locks, D via WAL fsync.
  • Postgres has no undo log: aborted row versions are just ignored then vacuumed.
  • Put invariants in the database (CHECK, UNIQUE, FK, EXCLUDE), not only in app code.
  • synchronous_commit = off can lose recent commits but never corrupts; fsync = off can corrupt.
  • Keep transactions short; set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout; long transactions cause bloat.
  • Never dual-write to DB and broker: use the outbox plus idempotent consumers.

questions.promptHtml: What is a database transaction, and what happens if you never write BEGIN?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know the unit of atomicity and autocommit behaviour, a frequent source of half-applied writes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit: BEGIN, then COMMIT to keep everything or ROLLBACK to discard it. Without BEGIN, Postgres wraps each single statement in its own tiny transaction (autocommit), so two statements in a script are not atomic together. In Postgres, once a statement errors inside a transaction, the transaction is aborted and every later statement fails until you ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
BEGIN -> UPDATE A (-100) -> UPDATE B (+100) -> COMMIT   both visible together
                              error here -> both undone
  • A transfer is two writes; if the server dies between them, money vanishes unless they share a transaction.
  • A transaction is a unit of work; locks are a mechanism inside it, not the definition.
  • Postgres DDL is transactional (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE can be rolled back); MySQL DDL implicitly commits.
  • State machine: idle, active, idle in transaction, idle in transaction (aborted).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "a transaction is a lock".
  • Assuming a script of separate statements is atomic.
  • Catching a SQL error in app code and carrying on in the same transaction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does autocommit do for a single UPDATE of 1M rows? -> One implicit transaction: all or nothing for that statement.
  2. Can you roll back DDL? -> In Postgres yes; in MySQL no.
  3. What does current transaction is aborted mean? -> A statement failed; Postgres refuses further commands until ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "BEGIN/COMMIT". Senior: autocommit semantics, the aborted state, transactional DDL, and where the transaction boundary belongs in app code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration script run without a transaction applied 3 of 5 steps before failing, leaving a half-migrated schema.

questions.promptHtml: What does each letter of ACID guarantee, and which mechanism in Postgres provides each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates recite ACID; seniors map each letter to a mechanism and know what can be relaxed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Atomicity: all or nothing, done with versioned rows and the commit log, so aborted versions are just ignored. Consistency: committed data obeys declared rules, via constraints, triggers and foreign keys; the database enforces only what you declare. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work, via MVCC snapshots and locks. Durability: committed data survives a crash, via the write-ahead log flushed with fsync before COMMIT returns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Letter Promise Postgres mechanism
A all or nothing MVCC tuple versions plus pg_xact
C rules hold constraints, FKs, triggers
I no interference snapshots plus locks
D survives crash WAL fsync
  • You can relax letters deliberately: synchronous_commit = off relaxes D (lose the last few hundred ms of commits, no corruption); lower isolation levels relax I.
  • ACID-C (rules hold) is not CAP-C (replicas agree/linearizability).
  • Many NoSQL stores give atomicity only per key, which is a heavier architectural decision.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing ACID consistency with CAP consistency.
  • Believing the database ensures business consistency without constraints.
  • Saying synchronous_commit = off can corrupt data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which letter does fsync serve? -> Durability.
  2. Which letter does an UNIQUE index serve? -> Consistency (and relies on isolation for concurrent inserts).
  3. What does fsync = off do? -> Can corrupt the cluster after a crash; never in production.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: four definitions. Senior: mechanisms, which dials exist, which are safe and the CAP-vs-ACID distinction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team turned off fsync to speed up CI-like loads on a staging DB, then promoted a snapshot of it to production data and hit corruption.

questions.contextHtml:
A signup handler checks uniqueness in code, and a wallet service checks balance in code:

def signup(email):
    if db.query("SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE email=%s", [email]):
        raise Conflict()
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES (%s)", [email])

def withdraw(acc, amt):
    bal = db.query_one("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=%s", [acc])
    if bal >= amt:
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance=%s WHERE id=%s", [bal-amt, acc])

Under load, support reports duplicate user rows with the same email and a few accounts with negative balances. Red herring: the team suspects clock skew.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix them properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a lock in the app" or "use a mutex"; misses that multiple app instances exist and that the DB should enforce the rule.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many app instances? What isolation level? Is there a UNIQUE index today?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Clean duplicates, then add the unique index; fix negative balances manually with an audit.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Check-then-act races: two requests pass the SELECT before either INSERT; read-modify-write overwrites in withdraw.
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT email, count(*) FROM users GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>1; Reproduce with two concurrent sessions.
  5. Root cause: The invariant lives only in app code, which cannot serialize across instances.
  6. Fix: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_uq ON users (email); and handle the unique violation; make the balance update atomic with a CHECK.
  7. Prevention: Declare invariants in the schema; review rule: "SELECT-then-INSERT for uniqueness is a bug".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: App-level locks do not cover other clients or scripts. Constraints cost a little write time but survive every future client.
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT bal_nonneg CHECK (balance >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE accounts VALIDATE CONSTRAINT bal_nonneg;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = 1;  -- fails with check violation when too low

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two concurrent withdrawals of 80 from 100? -> The second blocks, re-evaluates, sees 20, and the CHECK rejects it.
  • Soft-deleted users with reuse of email? -> Partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "unique by convention" username check allowed 300 duplicates during a viral signup spike; a unique index plus conflict handling ended it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds app-level locking.
  • Hire: unique index and atomic UPDATE with CHECK.
  • Strong hire: also handles NOT VALID/VALIDATE for existing data and partial unique cases.

questions.promptHtml: How does Postgres make a transaction atomic without an undo log, and what are the consequences?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand MVCC row versions and why Postgres has vacuum while InnoDB has undo.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Postgres never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE writes a new tuple version and marks the old one with the updater's xid in xmax. If the transaction aborts, readers consult the commit log (pg_xact), see it as aborted, and ignore the new version, so rollback is instant, even for a huge transaction. The consequence is dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim later. InnoDB instead updates in place and keeps undo, so rollback is slow but no vacuum is needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
version 1: xmin=100 xmax=205  balance=500   <- ended by tx 205
version 2: xmin=205 xmax=0    balance=400   <- new
tx 205 aborts: version 2 ignored, version 1 live again
  • xid is assigned when a transaction first writes (32-bit, wraparound is handled by freezing).
  • Visibility: xmin committed and visible to my snapshot, and xmax not.
  • Savepoints create subtransactions for partial rollback; they cost: over 64 live subtransactions per backend overflows a cache (pg_subtrans lookups), and long chains have caused real slowdowns.
  • Aborted rows consume space until vacuum.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id) VALUES (1, 7);
SAVEPOINT s1;
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, sku) VALUES (1, 'bad');  -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1;                                   -- order row kept
COMMIT;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming Postgres uses an undo log.
  • Wrapping every loop iteration in a savepoint.
  • Forgetting aborted work leaves bloat.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Postgres rollback fast? -> It only flips status in the commit log; no changes to replay backward.
  2. What's the downside of large aborted transactions? -> Dead tuples and index entries remain until vacuum.
  3. What happens near xid wraparound? -> Autovacuum freezes old tuples; failing to keep up forces the database into a protective shutdown/read-only mode (verify version behaviour).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "rolls back changes". Senior: no-undo design, xmin/xmax, commit log, vacuum consequence, savepoint cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A failed 200M-row bulk update rolled back instantly but left tens of GB of dead tuples that slowed queries until vacuum caught up.

questions.contextHtml:
An importer processes 5,000 rows per request. The framework wraps each row in a "nested transaction" (a savepoint) so one bad row can be skipped. After a traffic increase, throughput collapses: DB CPU 90%, many sessions waiting. pg_stat_activity (illustrative):

 wait_event_type | wait_event        | count
 LWLock          | SubtransSLRU      | 61
 LWLock          | SubtransBuffer    | 22

A separate report query runs for several minutes in a repeatable-read snapshot. Red herring: the team suspects the importer's rows are too wide.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add CPU" or "reduce row width"; does not recognise subtransaction overflow.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many savepoints per transaction? Any long-lived snapshots? Postgres version?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle the importer; end the long report snapshot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) more than 64 subtransactions per backend overflow the in-memory cache, forcing lookups in pg_subtrans (SLRU contention); (b) a long snapshot makes every visibility check consult subtrans; (c) row width (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: Wait events show SubtransSLRU; compare savepoint count in the importer; check oldest snapshot.
  5. Root cause: Thousands of savepoints per transaction plus a long snapshot turned visibility checks into shared-memory contention.
  6. Fix: Validate rows in the app or with a staging table and COPY; only use savepoints around genuinely risky statements; use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for expected conflicts, so no error and no savepoint is needed.
  7. Prevention: Framework config reviewed for implicit savepoints; alert on SLRU wait events; keep reports on replicas.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove error isolation, I would redesign it: batch validation and set-based inserts keep per-row skipping without subtransactions.
INSERT INTO imports (key, payload) VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need to know which rows failed? -> Insert into a staging table, run a set-based validation and report failures.
  • Is a single savepoint expensive? -> No; the problem is volume and long snapshots.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An ORM "nested transaction" in a loop looked harmless in dev (100 rows) and froze production at 50k rows per job.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales hardware.
  • Hire: identifies savepoint overflow.
  • Strong hire: replaces row-level savepoints with set-based patterns and prevents with alerts.

questions.subtopic: Adding constraints to a live table
questions.contextHtml: You must add a foreign key payments.order_id -> orders.id and CHECK (amount > 0) to payments (900M rows, 400 GB) on a live system doing 1,500 writes/s. Last time someone ran ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ... the table was locked for 11 minutes and the API timed out. Possibly ~0.02% of rows violate the rule (bad data from an old bug).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run ALTER in a maintenance window" or "just add it and see"; ignores NOT VALID, existing violators and lock queues.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we fix bad rows or must we tolerate them? Is there an index on payments.order_id? What is the lock_timeout policy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; no change yet. Count violators first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Adding a validated constraint scans the table under a strong lock; bad rows would make it fail after a long scan.
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE amount <= 0; and an anti-join for orphan order_ids on a replica.
  5. Root cause: Full validation requires reading 900M rows while holding a lock that blocks conflicting writes.
  6. Fix: Add constraints as NOT VALID (brief lock, enforces new writes only), clean bad rows in batches, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (takes a lighter lock that does not block normal reads/writes, verify for FKs on your version). Ensure an index on the referencing column first so deletes on the parent are cheap.
  7. Prevention: Migration tooling that rejects blocking DDL, lock_timeout on every migration, and retry with backoff.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: NOT VALID leaves old violators until cleaned; I accept this temporarily. I would not drop the constraint to "unblock" a migration once validated.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT payments_amount_pos CHECK (amount > 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT payments_order_fk FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) NOT VALID;
-- fix bad rows in batches, then:
ALTER TABLE payments VALIDATE CONSTRAINT payments_amount_pos;
ALTER TABLE payments VALIDATE CONSTRAINT payments_order_fk;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The ALTER waits behind a long transaction and blocks all others? -> Lock queue effect; the lock_timeout and retry avoids queuing everyone behind it.
  • Deferrable FK? -> Only if circular inserts require checking at COMMIT.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single ALTER without lock_timeout waited for an idle-in-transaction session and blocked every write for 14 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: plain ALTER in a window.
  • Hire: NOT VALID then VALIDATE.
  • Strong hire: cleans data, adds lock_timeout/retry, indexes FK column and explains lock queues.

questions.promptHtml: What does COMMIT actually guarantee in Postgres, and what do synchronous_commit and fsync change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates "writes go to disk" folklore from the WAL model and its real trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: COMMIT returns only after the commit WAL record is flushed (fsync) to disk; the table pages are written later by checkpoints and are recoverable from WAL. synchronous_commit = off returns before the flush: a crash can lose the last few hundred milliseconds of commits but never corrupts data. fsync = off can corrupt the whole cluster. With synchronous replicas, remote_write, on or remote_apply decide how far the commit must propagate before acknowledgement.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> COMMIT -> WAL buffer -> fsync WAL -> ack
(later) checkpoint writes dirty heap pages; crash recovery replays WAL
  • One session doing small commits is limited by fsync latency: ~0.5 to 2 ms per fsync on cloud SSD means ~500 to 2,000 commits/s.
  • Group commit lets concurrent sessions share one fsync, so 64 sessions reach tens of thousands/s.
  • synchronous_commit = off loses up to about 3 x wal_writer_delay (200 ms default) of commits.
  • Hardware matters: drives that acknowledge fsync without persisting (no power-loss protection) silently break durability.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off;   -- per transaction, for low-value data like click events

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying COMMIT writes table pages to disk.
  • Thinking asynchronous commit can corrupt.
  • Ignoring that a synchronous standby adds a network round trip to every commit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How can I get durability and throughput? -> Batch, rely on group commit, use fast WAL storage.
  2. Is synchronous_commit per-session? -> Yes, it can be set per transaction, so only low-value writes opt out.
  3. What does remote_apply give? -> Read-your-writes on the standby at extra latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "WAL is written first". Senior: flush semantics, group commit, per-transaction control, hardware caveats and replica sync modes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Payments kept on with a synchronous standby; analytics ingestion used off per transaction and avoided a 5x commit latency penalty.

questions.contextHtml: A nightly job loads 20M rows with a loop issuing one INSERT per row in autocommit mode. It runs 3 hours at ~1,800 rows/s. CPU is 15%, disk write bandwidth is low but pg_stat_wal shows wal_sync count ~1,800/s. Storage is a cloud SSD with ~0.5 ms fsync. Red herring: the team wants a larger instance.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Bigger instance, or fsync = off.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the load be all-or-nothing? Is the table indexed heavily? Can duplicates occur (idempotent re-runs)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap 5,000 rows per transaction.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One fsync per row (autocommit) bounds throughput near 1/(fsync latency); round trips; index maintenance.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_wal sync counters, test throughput with batch sizes 1k, 5k, 10k.
  5. Root cause: 1.8k rows/s is 1.8k commits/s, i.e. the commit rate limit of a sequential session (~0.5 ms each), not CPU.
  6. Fix: Use COPY (often 10x or more faster than row INSERTs) or multi-row inserts in 1k to 10k batches; load into an unlogged/staging table then insert-select; drop and rebuild nonessential indexes for a one-time load; run ANALYZE afterwards.
  7. Prevention: Loader template with batching and idempotent keys; load-test with realistic fsync latency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Larger batches mean larger rollback blast radius and longer-held locks; 1k to 10k is a good range. I would not turn off fsync; synchronous_commit = off for this session is an option if losing the last few batches on a crash is acceptable and the job is restartable.
COPY readings (device_id, ts, value) FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv);
-- or: batches of 5000 rows inside BEGIN ... COMMIT

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A failure at row 15M? -> Commit in chunks with a checkpoint table or ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING so the job resumes.
  • Parallel loaders? -> Group commit helps; watch index contention.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "slow ETL" ran 6 hours for years; a single BEGIN/COMMIT per 10k rows cut it to 25 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bigger box or fsync off.
  • Hire: batching or COPY.
  • Strong hire: explains fsync-per-commit math, resumability and post-load ANALYZE.

questions.promptHtml: Why are long-running and idle-in-transaction sessions dangerous in Postgres, and what guardrails do you set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: One of the most common causes of surprise bloat and lock pileups.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A transaction keeps its snapshot, so VACUUM cannot remove dead row versions newer than the oldest open snapshot (the xmin horizon). It also holds locks, blocking others. An idle in transaction session does nothing yet keeps both. I keep transactions short, never hold them across HTTP calls or user think time, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout, plus monitor the oldest xact_start.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
idle tx (old snapshot) -> VACUUM can't clean newer dead rows -> bloat -> slower scans, bigger indexes
                      -> holds locks -> others queue -> pool exhausts
  • Also blocks DDL: an ALTER TABLE waiting on a lock queues every later query behind it.
  • Replication: long queries on standbys can conflict with replay (hot_standby_feedback trade-off).
  • Poolers in transaction mode break session-level features.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT pid, state, now()-xact_start AS age, left(query,60)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE app SET statement_timeout = '15s';

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling a remote API inside an open transaction.
  • Not setting idle-in-transaction timeouts.
  • Keeping analytic queries on the primary for hours.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does one idle transaction affect unrelated tables? -> The xmin horizon is database-wide (cluster-wide for some catalogs), so cleanup is held back everywhere.
  2. What do you alert on? -> Oldest transaction age, n_dead_tup, table size growth.
  3. How does this interact with DDL? -> Lock queue: a waiting ALTER blocks new readers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "long transactions block". Senior: the horizon concept, bloat mechanism, timeouts, DDL lock queues and replica feedback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crashed worker left a transaction idle for 6 hours; the 20 GB table grew to 35 GB and index scans slowed.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. Over a weekend the orders table grew from 20 GB to 62 GB; p99 for order lookups tripled; autovacuum showed as constantly running but n_dead_tup kept rising. Evidence (illustrative):

 pid  | state               | age      | query
 8812 | idle in transaction | 41:12:07 | SELECT * FROM report_cache WHERE ...
 
 relname | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | last_autovacuum
 orders  | 52,000,000 | 38,000,000 | 3 min ago

Red herring: someone raised autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit and saw no improvement.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, remediation and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Tune autovacuum harder" or "run VACUUM FULL now".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What opened pid 8812 and why is it idle? Is hot_standby_feedback on with a stuck replica query? Replication slots lagging?
  2. Immediate mitigation: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(8812); then watch autovacuum finish; check replication slots as well.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: An old snapshot pins the xmin horizon (dominant: the 41 hours matches the growth); also check prepared transactions and inactive replication slots; autovacuum speed (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_activity (oldest xact), pg_replication_slots, pg_prepared_xacts; after termination, n_dead_tup should fall with vacuum progress in pg_stat_progress_vacuum.
  5. Root cause: A service crashed mid-request leaving a connection idle in a transaction; VACUUM ran but could not remove tuples newer than that snapshot.
  6. Fix: Terminate, let vacuum catch up; if bloat remains, rebuild with pg_repack or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rather than VACUUM FULL (exclusive lock).
  7. Prevention: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout='30s' for app roles, a dashboard and page for oldest transaction age > 5 min, app code reviewing connection handling (always rollback in finally), TCP keepalives.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Timeouts will occasionally kill legitimate slow sessions; give batch roles different limits. I would not make vacuum more aggressive until the blocker is gone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The idle session was a human in psql? -> Same timeout plus guidance and read-only roles.
  • A stuck logical replication slot? -> It also holds the horizon (and WAL); drop it if it is dead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A notebook left BEGIN; open on a Friday; the table doubled by Monday; two lines of config ended the class of incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes autovacuum.
  • Hire: finds the old snapshot and terminates it.
  • Strong hire: checks slots/prepared xacts, cleans bloat safely, and adds timeouts and alerts.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you atomically write to Postgres and publish to Kafka, and how do the transactional outbox and idempotency fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Dual writes are a classic senior-level correctness trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A database transaction cannot include the broker, so saving then publishing can leave one succeeded and the other failed. With the outbox I write the business row and an outbox row in the same local transaction, and a relay (polling or CDC like Debezium) publishes outbox rows and marks them sent. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent, usually with a dedupe key or a unique constraint. End-to-end exactly-once does not exist; at-least-once plus idempotency approximates it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Service -> [orders row + outbox row] one tx -> Relay -> Kafka -> Consumer (idempotent)
  • Failure windows with dual write: publish fails after commit (lost event) or commit fails after publish (phantom event).
  • Relay polling: SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100, then publish, then mark sent. A crash between publish and mark causes re-publish, hence duplicates.
  • Ordering: per-aggregate ordering requires partition key = aggregate id and relay ordering.
  • Alternatives: sagas with compensations, or 2PC (heavy, blocking, rarely worth it).
  • Outbox table needs cleanup (partition or delete sent rows).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, total) VALUES (42, 7, 99.00);
INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, type, payload) VALUES (42, 'OrderCreated', '{"id":42}');
COMMIT;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving and then publishing with no outbox.
  • Claiming exactly-once delivery end to end.
  • Outbox rows never cleaned, and the relay scanning an ever-growing table.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why SKIP LOCKED? -> Multiple relays can claim different rows without blocking each other.
  2. How does CDC differ from polling? -> Reads the WAL, lower latency and no polling load, but needs replication slot management.
  3. How do consumers dedupe? -> Store processed event ids with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the side effect.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use the outbox". Senior: failure windows, at-least-once, ordering, relay concurrency, cleanup and slot hazards in CDC.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service that published to a queue after commit lost events during deploy restarts; adding an outbox removed the gaps.

questions.contextHtml:
Checkout does: (1) INSERT INTO orders and COMMIT, (2) POST to the Inventory service, (3) publish OrderCreated to Kafka. Every week a few dozen orders exist with no inventory reservation or no email event. The code is:

def checkout(cart):
    order_id = db.insert_order(cart)      # commits
    inventory.reserve(order_id, cart)     # HTTP, sometimes times out
    kafka.send("OrderCreated", order_id)  # sometimes the pod is killed first

The team debates three options: 2PC across services, a saga, or the outbox. Volume is 400 orders/s; the inventory API is owned by another team.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you pick and how do you roll it out?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries" or "wrap it all in a transaction"; ignores that HTTP and Kafka are outside the DB transaction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the reservation succeed before confirming the order? Is the inventory call idempotent? What ordering guarantees are needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A reconciliation job that finds orders without events/reservations and repairs them, to fix the existing gaps.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Crash/timeouts between steps leave inconsistent state (dual writes); retries without idempotency could double-reserve.
  4. How I'd verify: Query for orders without reservation records; inject failures between steps in a test.
  5. Root cause: Three systems updated without a shared atomic boundary.
  6. Fix: Outbox in the checkout transaction (order row plus OrderCreated and ReserveInventory outbox rows). A relay publishes to Kafka; the inventory consumer is idempotent keyed by order_id. If reservation can fail for business reasons, model it as a saga: order PENDING, then CONFIRMED or CANCELLED via compensating event.
  7. Prevention: Failure-injection tests, invariant monitor (orders without reservation older than 5 minutes), idempotency keys on every cross-service call.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: 2PC adds blocking and coordinator failure modes and the inventory team likely cannot support it. The outbox adds latency (tens to hundreds of ms) and eventual consistency, which I accept.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Outbox relay lags? -> Alert on oldest unsent row; multiple relays with SKIP LOCKED.
  • Customer sees "confirmed" before inventory? -> Show PENDING state until the saga completes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reconciliation job found 0.3% of orders orphaned; after outbox adoption the orphan count was zero for a year, with one planned incident when the relay lagged.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries around dual writes.
  • Hire: outbox with idempotent consumers.
  • Strong hire: saga modelling, reconciliation, invariants monitoring and justified rejection of 2PC.

questions.contextHtml:
A new "audit events" service must have "zero data loss" per the compliance lead, and also "p99 under 5 ms per write" per product. It writes 8,000 events/s, single region, Postgres on cloud NVMe with 1 ms fsync, one synchronous standby in another AZ (2 ms RTT). Initial benchmarks:

-- illustrative
synchronous_commit=on  + sync standby, 1 client:  p99 6.1 ms, 160 commits/s per connection
synchronous_commit=off:                           p99 0.4 ms

A developer proposes synchronous_commit=off "since Postgres never corrupts". Another proposes fsync=off.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks off and says "durability is fine", or fsync=off.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "zero loss" mean: loss of acknowledged writes on a single node failure? Can clients retry unacknowledged writes? Is the 5 ms budget end-to-end or DB only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; this is a design decision. Do not ship off for audit data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The latency target and sync replication conflict at 1 client; concurrency and group commit change throughput; the requirement may be flexible (e.g. ack after local + standby flush).
  4. How I'd verify: Benchmark with 64 concurrent connections; measure remote_write vs on vs remote_apply.
  5. Root cause of the tension: Durability across node loss requires a network round trip plus fsync per commit.
  6. Fix: Keep synchronous_commit = on with a synchronous standby (quorum ANY 1), get throughput via concurrency, group commit and batching in a queue; negotiate the SLO to p99 ~7 to 8 ms for writes, or make the client ack from an app-level durable queue. Use off only for non-audit data per transaction.
  7. Prevention: Document per-table durability class; test failover (RPO = 0) quarterly; verify the drives honour fsync (power-loss protection).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: fsync = off can corrupt the cluster, never acceptable. synchronous_commit = off loses the last ~hundreds of ms on a crash, which violates "zero loss".
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_a, standby_b)';
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_commit = 'on';

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Standby goes down? -> With one sync standby, writes stall; use a quorum of 2 candidates, accepting the design cost.
  • Region failure? -> A cross-region sync would add tens of ms; accept RPO > 0 or move to a consensus store.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "durable" setting was silently off on a replica-restore, found only in a failover test where 400 ms of audit events vanished.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables fsync or sets off.
  • Hire: sync commit with standby, understands the trade.
  • Strong hire: negotiates the requirement, quantifies, uses concurrency and quorum and tests failover.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments API supports an Idempotency-Key header. The implementation:

def charge(key, req):
    prior = db.query("SELECT response FROM idem WHERE key=%s", [key])
    if prior: return prior
    resp = psp.charge(req)                 # external, 2 s latency
    db.execute("INSERT INTO idem(key, response) VALUES (%s,%s)", [key, resp])
    return resp

After a mobile client retried aggressively on a slow network, 41 customers were charged twice. Logs show two requests with the same key 1.3 s apart, both finding no prior row. A UNIQUE index exists on idem.key; the second INSERT failed with a unique violation after the PSP charged, and the API returned 500.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The unique index should have prevented it" or "add a retry on 500"; misses the check-then-act race around the external call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the PSP support idempotency keys? How long can a request run? What is the key scope (per merchant)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Refund the 41 duplicates; temporarily serialize by key or lower client retry rate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Concurrent requests with the same key race: both pass the SELECT; the unique index only protects the response record, not the external charge.
  4. How I'd verify: Correlate logs by key and timestamp; check the PSP for two charges; reproduce with two parallel calls.
  5. Root cause: The uniqueness claim is made after the side effect. The reservation of the key must happen before charging.
  6. Fix: Insert the key first with status IN_PROGRESS (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING); only the winner calls the PSP, passing the same key to the PSP; concurrent duplicates get 409 or wait/poll for the stored result; update the row to DONE with the response; recover stuck IN_PROGRESS rows via a timeout job that queries the PSP by key.
  7. Prevention: Concurrency test that fires N identical requests; store request hash with key to reject key reuse with a different body; monitor duplicate charges.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Holding a DB transaction across the 2 s PSP call is a long-transaction hazard; use the status-row pattern instead. I would not rely on client-side behaviour.
INSERT INTO idem (key, status, request_hash) VALUES ($1, 'IN_PROGRESS', $2)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING key;
-- 0 rows returned => someone else owns it: return stored result or 409

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The pod dies after the PSP call but before DONE? -> Recovery job asks the PSP for the charge by idempotency key and completes the row.
  • Same key, different amount? -> Compare request hash; return 422.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Double charges appeared only for slow mobile clients; a "claim then act" idempotency table made retries safe and refund tickets stopped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on the unique index after the side effect.
  • Hire: claims key first with ON CONFLICT and uses PSP idempotency.
  • Strong hire: handles in-progress state, crash recovery, request-hash checks and avoids long transactions.
